analysis.one_liner: Requires cell phone carriers to alert customers before overage charges and get consent first.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced with no cosponsors, was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the 112th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have directed the FCC to write rules requiring wireless carriers to warn subscribers free of charge when they have used 80% of their monthly voice, text, or data allowance, and to get the customer's permission before charging for service beyond that limit [S2][S3]. Its findings cite an FCC survey finding that 1 in 6 mobile subscribers has experienced 'bill shock,' a sudden unexplained jump in the monthly bill [S3]. The bill never advanced beyond committee referral [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Cell phone subscribers on capped service plans, who would be warned before hitting their monthly limit and could not be charged for going over it unless they first agreed, with the alerts and consent messages themselves provided at no cost and not counted against their plan [S2][S3].

how_it_helps.text: Carriers must send a free voice, text, or email alert when a subscriber has used 80% of the monthly limit for minutes, texts, or data, and the alert itself does not count against the plan [S3].
Carriers must obtain the subscriber's consent before allowing or charging for service beyond the monthly limit, so no one is billed for overages they never asked for [S2][S3].
The bill's findings state that an FCC survey found 1 in 6 mobile subscribers has experienced bill shock and that most receive no notification before or after a sudden bill increase [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Wireless carriers, which would lose some of the overage-fee revenue they collect when customers exceed their plan limits without realizing it, and would bear the cost of building and sending the free alerts and consent requests [S2][S3].

drawbacks.text: A hard consent requirement could cut off service for customers who actually want to keep using data or minutes past their limit, unless they happen to respond to the alert; someone relying on their phone could be interrupted mid-use [S3].

The bill sets a uniform federal mandate rather than trusting market competition; carriers already offered some usage tools voluntarily, and the mandate applies even to customers who never experience bill shock [S2].
The costs of the alert and consent systems fall on carriers, which may pass them through to all subscribers, including customers who never exceed their limits [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real but targeted: it protects the sizable minority who get hit with surprise overage charges, at a modest cost to carriers in foregone overage fees and alert systems. The consent requirement is the bluntest part of the design, since it can interrupt service for customers who would have gladly paid, but the bill lets customers consent in advance at no cost, which softens that problem. On balance a modest, well-aimed consumer protection with a manageable design tradeoff.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee the day it was introduced, and with no cosponsors and no committee action of any kind, it died there when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Tom Udall (D-NM) introduced the Cell Phone Bill Shock Act of 2011 in the Senate on April 5, 2011 [S1][S5].
The same day, it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation [S5].
No cosponsors ever signed on to the bill [S4].
The committee took no further action, and the bill received no markup, floor vote, or consideration before the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013 [S5][S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Wireless carriers, which kept collecting overage fees without a federal consent requirement; consumers got nothing from this bill, though the FCC separately pursued its own bill-shock alert rules around the same time.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Wireless carriers kept their overage fees

for.name: Tom Udall
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks, but drew no cosponsors.

against.name: Jay Rockefeller
against.role: Chair, Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee
against.what_they_did: As chair of the committee the bill was referred to, never brought it to a hearing, markup, or vote; the record shows no committee action after referral.

against.name: Wireless carriers
against.role: Mobile service providers facing a consent mandate on overage fees
against.what_they_did: The bill would have required their consent before overage billing; no carrier or trade group supported the bill and none cosponsored it.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Democratic sponsor and zero cosponsors of either party, so it never developed a partisan profile; no vote was ever taken.

industries.note: The bill would have required free 80%-used alerts and customer consent before overage charges, cutting into the overage fees carriers collect from customers who exceed plan limits unknowingly. Carriers' revenue from surprise overages ran directly against the customers the bill was protecting.
